name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.

The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** A background fork's tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. It sends a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching a background fork, you know nothing about what it found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the feature flag is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, feature flag wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

`cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Shell state does not persist. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# candidate's source to decide anything.

# Write plain shell commands here; no quoting of the whole block is needed.

  # using playwright-core's API directly. Point it at the exact Chromium build pinned by (and

  node make build 2>&1 | tail -n 300

  GREP_ARGS=()
  for id in "${IDS[@]}"; do
    esc=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write(process.argv[1].replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&"))' "$id")
    GREP_ARGS+=("--grep=^${esc}\$")

  # and assert on the geometry of what is drawn, with no stored layout or image snapshots.

  GEN_STATUS=$?

    echo "FATAL: gen_junit.mjs failed with status $GEN_STATUS" >&2
    exit $GEN_STATUS
  fi
}

# candidate cannot replace the harness. Space-separated, relative to /app; '' if none.

STDOUT_LOG=/logs/verifier/test-stdout.txt
STDERR_LOG=/logs/verifier/test-stderr.txt
export JUNIT_OUT=/logs/verifier/junit.xml
export TEST_IDS_FILE=/logs/verifier/test_ids.txt
: > "$STDOUT_LOG"; : > "$STDERR_LOG"
rm -f "$JUNIT_OUT" /logs/verifier/reward.txt /logs/verifier/reward.json

#

# generated bundles) is untracked. A bare `add -A` would capture all of it. Inverting it -- stage
# tracked modifications, then add only untracked files that LOOK like source -- keeps the agent's

# look like source -- so an agent adding config.yml, a .cmake module or an extensionless script
# loses it, and the patch still looks clean. That is the failure this manifest exists to expose.
#

# Build artifacts are excluded by the same rules as the capture, to keep the list readable.

    ':(exclude)lib/' ':(exclude)build/' ':(exclude).deps/' \
    ':(exclude)*.o' ':(exclude)*.d' ':(exclude)*.a' ':(exclude)*.lo' ':(exclude)*.la' \
    ':(exclude)*.so' ':(exclude)*.so.*' ':(exclude)*.gch' ':(exclude)*.pyc' 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -vxF -f "$_SUBCAP" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
{ echo "# Untracked files NOT captured into submission.patch, newest first."
  echo "# Anything the agent created sorts above build output, which predates the agent phase."
  echo "# total: ${_SUBSKIPN}  (showing at most 40)"

      ':(exclude)lib/' ':(exclude)build/' ':(exclude).deps/' \
      ':(exclude)*.o' ':(exclude)*.d' ':(exclude)*.a' ':(exclude)*.lo' ':(exclude)*.la' \
      ':(exclude)*.so' ':(exclude)*.so.*' ':(exclude)*.gch' ':(exclude)*.pyc' 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -vxF -f "$_SUBCAP" 2>/dev/null | head -200 \
    | while IFS= read -r _f; do
        printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$(stat -c %Y "/app/$_f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" \
                              "$(stat -c %s "/app/$_f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" "$_f"
      done \
    | sort -rn | head -40 | awk -F'\t' '{printf "%s\t%s\t%s\n",$1,$2,$3}'

# Size guard. The whitelist is a heuristic, so a task laying out source unusually could still
# produce something enormous. Cap it and leave a diagnosable stub: a truncated capture is
# recoverable, a full disk is not.
_SUBSZ=$(wc -c < "$_SUB" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)

    echo "Directories contributing to the discarded patch:"

  : > "$_SUB"
  echo "== submission.patch SUPPRESSED (${_SUBSZ} bytes > 5MB cap) ==" | tee -a "$STDOUT_LOG"

    | tee -a "$STDOUT_LOG"
fi


# 1. Restore every path test.patch touches. Both diff headers are read, so new files, binary
#    baselines (image-comparison PNGs, snapshots), renames and deletions are all covered.
_patch_paths=$( { sed -n 's#^diff --git a/\(.*\) b/.*#\1#p' /tests/test.patch
                  sed -n 's#^diff --git a/.* b/\(.*\)#\1#p' /tests/test.patch; } | sort -u )
for _p in $_patch_paths; do
  git -C /app checkout harbor_base -- "$_p" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "/app/$_p" 2>/dev/null || true
done
for _d in $PROTECTED_DIRS; do
  git -C /app checkout harbor_base -- "$_d" 2>/dev/null || true
  git -C /app clean -fdq -- "$_d" 2>/dev/null || true
done

# 2. Apply the hidden tests.
echo "== applying test.patch ==" | tee -a "$STDOUT_LOG"
git apply --binary /tests/test.patch 2>>"$STDERR_LOG" \
  || git apply /tests/test.patch 2>>"$STDERR_LOG" \
  || patch -p1 -i /tests/test.patch 2>>"$STDERR_LOG" \
  || { echo "ERROR: could not apply test.patch" | tee -a "$STDERR_LOG"; exit 1; }

c = json.load(open("/tests/config.json"))
print("\n".join(c["f2p"] + c["p2p"]))

  || echo "(tests exited non-zero; parsing the report)" | tee -a "$STDOUT_LOG"

# The `|| echo ""` is load-bearing: the judge must never be able to fail the run.
RUBRIC=""

  RUBRIC=$(python3 /tests/judge.py --rubrics /tests/rubrics.json --repo /app \
             2>/logs/verifier/judge.log || echo "")
  echo "Rubric verdict: ${RUBRIC:-pending (judge request written; rescore after grading)}"

_CANON_TXT = "/logs/verifier/reward.txt"

    tests_passed is 1.0 only when every f2p test passes AND every p2p test still passes. A
    strict subset of f2p passing is not partial progress worth scoring: the task is unsolved,

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Turn the JUnit report into the task reward.

The reward is binary: 1.0 only when every configured f2p and p2p test is found exactly once in the
report and passed; otherwise 0.0. f2p_passed / f2p_total and p2p_passed / p2p_total record how close
a run came. The verifier reads test outcomes only, never the candidate's source.
"""
import html
import json
import os
import sys
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

CONF = json.load(open("/tests/config.json"))
F2P, P2P = CONF["f2p"], CONF["p2p"]
REPORT = os.environ.get("JUNIT_OUT", "/logs/verifier/junit.xml")
OUT_DIR = "/logs/verifier"


import atexit
import json as _cj
import os as _co
import sys as _cs

_CANON_JSON = "/logs/verifier/reward.json"
_CANON_TXT = "/logs/verifier/reward.txt"
_canon = {}


def canon_reward(f2p_passed, f2p_total, p2p_passed, p2p_total, rubric):
    """THE reward policy for the whole corpus. BINARY -- there is no partial credit.

    tests_passed is 1.0 only when every f2p test passes AND every p2p test still passes. A
    strict subset of f2p passing is not partial progress worth scoring: the task is unsolved,
    so it is 0.0.

    reward is the same value, zeroed when the rubric judge failed a criterion. A "pass" or a
    "not graded" verdict never lowers the score -- the judge must never be able to penalise a
    run it could not grade.
    """
    f, t = int(f2p_passed), int(f2p_total)
    p, q = int(p2p_passed), int(p2p_total)
    solved = bool(t) and f == t and p == q
    tests_passed = 1.0 if solved else 0.0
    _canon.clear()
    _canon.update({
        "reward": 0.0 if rubric == "fail" else tests_passed,
        "tests_passed": tests_passed,
        "f2p_passed": f, "f2p_total": t,
        "p2p_passed": p, "p2p_total": q,
        "rubric_passed": {"pass": 1, "fail": 0}.get(rubric, -1),
    })
    return _canon["reward"]


@atexit.register
def _canon_flush():
    if not _canon:
        return
    try:
        _co.makedirs(_co.path.dirname(_CANON_JSON), exist_ok=True)
        with open(_CANON_JSON, "w") as _h:
            _cj.dump(_canon, _h, indent=2)
        # reward.txt too: harbor prefers reward.json, but the sandbox teardown script and the
        # lighthouse UI read reward.txt. Writing both from one dict means they cannot disagree.
        with open(_CANON_TXT, "w") as _h:
            _h.write(str(_canon["reward"]))
    except Exception as _exc:
        print("WARNING: could not write %s: %s" % (_CANON_JSON, _exc), file=_cs.stderr)


def rubric_verdict(argv):
    """The verdict test.sh hands in as `--rubric pass|fail|""`.

    Anything that is not an explicit pass/fail -- including the empty string test.sh passes
    when judge.py wrote no verdict -- means "not graded", which must never penalise the run.
    """
    if "--rubric" not in argv:
        return None
    i = argv.index("--rubric")
    value = argv[i + 1].strip().lower() if i + 1 < len(argv) else ""
    return value if value in ("pass", "fail") else None


def load_junit(path):
    """Every reported test, keyed by "classname name" and by name; a key seen twice with different
    outcomes counts as failed."""
    results = {}
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return results
    try:
        root = ET.parse(path).getroot()
    except ET.ParseError:
        return results
    for tc in root.iter("testcase"):
        tags = {c.tag for c in tc}
        outcome = "skip" if "skipped" in tags else ("fail" if tags & {"failure", "error"} else "pass")
        full = f"{tc.get('classname', '')} {tc.get('name', '')}".strip()
        for key in {full, tc.get("name", "")}:
            if key in results and results[key] != outcome:
                results[key] = "fail"
            else:
                results[key] = outcome
    return results


def junit_key(test_id):
    """A pytest node id (tests/test_x.py::TestA::test_b[png]) as the JUnit report names it
    ("tests.test_x.TestA test_b[png]"); other ids unchanged."""
    if "::" not in test_id:
        return test_id
    parts = test_id.split("::")
    mod = parts[0][:-3] if parts[0].endswith(".py") else parts[0]
    return f"{'.'.join([mod.replace('/', '.')] + parts[1:-1])} {parts[-1]}"


def resolve(test_id, results):
    """The outcome of one configured test: an exact key match first (the id as written, or a
    pytest node id in JUnit form), else the single reported test whose key ends with it. Missing
    or ambiguous counts as not passed."""
    keys = [test_id, junit_key(test_id)]
    if " :: " in test_id:  # "file :: describe › test" (playwright list output)
        keys.append(test_id.replace(" :: ", " ", 1))
    if " > " in test_id:  # "describe > test": jest-junit joins with a space, playwright with " › "
        head, rest = test_id.split(" > ", 1)
        keys += [test_id.replace(" > ", " "), test_id.replace(" > ", " › "), head + " " + rest.replace(" > ", " › ")]
    keys += [k.replace('"', "") for k in keys]  # jest-junit drops quotation marks from names
    keys += [html.unescape(k) for k in keys]  # an id copied from a JUnit file may keep ' "
    keys = list(dict.fromkeys(keys))
    for key in keys:
        if key in results:
            return results[key]
    for key in keys:
        hits = {k: v for k, v in results.items() if k.endswith(key)}
        if hits and len(set(hits.values())) == 1:
            return next(iter(hits.values()))
        if hits:
            return "ambiguous"
    # "file > test" with a describe level left out: a test in that file whose name ends the same
    parts = test_id.split(" > ")
    if len(parts) >= 2 and ("." in parts[0] or "/" in parts[0]):
        hits = {k: v for k, v in results.items() if k.startswith(parts[0] + " ") and k.endswith(parts[-1])}
        if hits and len(set(hits.values())) == 1:
            return next(iter(hits.values()))
        if hits:
            return "ambiguous"
    return "missing"


def main():
    results = load_junit(REPORT)
    detail = {}
    f2p_ok = 0
    for t in F2P:
        r = resolve(t, results)
        detail[f"f2p::{t}"] = r
        f2p_ok += r == "pass"
    p2p_ok = 0
    for t in P2P:
        r = resolve(t, results)
        detail[f"p2p::{t}"] = r
        p2p_ok += r == "pass"
    canon_reward(f2p_ok, len(F2P), p2p_ok, len(P2P), rubric_verdict(sys.argv[1:]))
    os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    json.dump(detail, open(f"{OUT_DIR}/reward_detail.json", "w"), indent=2)
    print(json.dumps(_canon))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

+// Generates a JUnit XML report for a fixed set of bokehjs devtools tests,
+// possibly spanning multiple suites (unit/integration/defaults).
+// Usage: node gen_junit.mjs <tests.json> <junit_out> <repo_bokehjs_dir> <logs_dir>
+//   tests.json: [{"id": "full test description", "file": "...", "suite": "unit"}]
+//   logs_dir: contains "<suite>.log" for every suite referenced in tests.json
+import fs from "node:fs"
+import path from "node:path"
+
+const [,, testsJsonPath, junitOut, repoDir, logsDir] = process.argv
+
+const tests = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(testsJsonPath, "utf-8"))
+
+function xmlEscape(s) {
+  return String(s).replace(/[<>&'"]/g, (c) => ({
+    "<": "<", ">": ">", "&": "&", "'": "'", '"': """,
+  }[c]))
+}
+
+const BASELINE_SUITES = new Set(["integration", "defaults"])
+
+function resultsForSuite(suite) {
+  const resultsById = new Map()
+  if (BASELINE_SUITES.has(suite)) {
+    const candidates = ["report.jsonl", "report.json"].map((n) => path.join(repoDir, "test", "baselines", "linux", n))
+    const reportPath = candidates.find((p) => fs.existsSync(p))
+    if (reportPath == null) {
+      console.error(`FATAL: expected a report at one of ${JSON.stringify(candidates)} but none exist (suite=${suite})`)
+      process.exit(97)
+    }
+    if (reportPath.endsWith(".jsonl")) {
+      const lines = fs.readFileSync(reportPath, "utf-8").split("\n").filter((l) => l.trim() !== "")
+      for (const line of lines) {
+        const record = JSON.parse(line)
+        if (record.type === "result") {
+          resultsById.set(record.descriptions.join(" "), !!record.status.success)
+        }
+      }
+    } else {
+      const report = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(reportPath, "utf-8"))
+      for (const [descriptions, status] of report.results) {
+        resultsById.set(descriptions.join(" "), !!status.success)
+      }
+    }
+  } else {
+    // Parse "Failed tests:" section from the plain-text log (FORCE_COLOR=0).
+    const logFile = path.join(logsDir, `${suite}.log`)
+    if (!fs.existsSync(logFile)) {
+      console.error(`FATAL: expected log at ${logFile} but it doesn't exist (suite=${suite})`)
+      process.exit(97)
+    }
+    const log = fs.readFileSync(logFile, "utf-8")
+    // eslint-disable-next-line no-control-regex
+    const plain = log.replace(/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m/g, "")
+    const failed = new Set()
+
+    // Primary signal: inline failure trees printed as each test runs, e.g.:
+    //   ✗ Bug
+    //    └┬─ in issue #15712
+    //     └── renders wedges with ... as full discs
+    // (works across devtools versions, even ones without a trailing "Failed tests:" summary)
+    const lines = plain.split("\n")
+    for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
+      const head = /^\s*✗\s(.*)$/.exec(lines[i]) // ✗
+      if (head == null) continue
+      const parts = [head[1]]
+      let j = i + 1
+      for (; j < lines.length; j++) {
+        const node = /^\s*└(?:──|┬─)\s(.*)$/.exec(lines[j]) // └── or └┬─
+        if (node == null) break
+        parts.push(node[1])
+      }
+      failed.add(parts.join(" "))
+      i = j - 1
+    }
+
+    // Secondary signal: a trailing "Failed tests:" summary, if this devtools version has one.
+    const idx = plain.lastIndexOf("Failed tests:")
+    if (idx !== -1) {
+      const tail = plain.slice(idx + "Failed tests:".length)
+      for (const rawLine of tail.split("\n").slice(1)) {
+        if (rawLine.trim() === "") break
+        let line = rawLine.replace(/^\s+/, "").replace(/\s+$/, "")
+        line = line.replace(/\s*\(timeout\)$/, "")
+        if (line !== "") failed.add(line)
+      }
+    }
+
+    // A log only names the tests that failed, so a test that never ran (a build error, a test file
+    // that failed to load, a grep that matched nothing) would otherwise read as passed. Count a
+    // suite's tests as passed only when the runner's own summary accounts for every one of them.
+    const expected = tests.filter((t) => t.suite === suite).length
+    const summaries = [...plain.matchAll(/(?:(\d+) failed, )?(\d+) passed, (\d+) skipped, (\d+) deselected of total (\d+) tests/g)]
+    const summary = summaries.at(-1)
+    const n_failed = summary == null ? 0 : Number(summary[1] ?? 0)
+    const n_passed = summary == null ? 0 : Number(summary[2])
+    const n_skipped = summary == null ? 0 : Number(summary[3])
+    const attributed = tests.filter((t) => t.suite === suite && failed.has(t.id)).length
+    const complete = summary != null && n_failed + n_passed === expected && n_skipped === 0 && attributed === n_failed
+    if (!complete) {
+      console.error(`suite=${suite}: runner summary ${summary == null ? "missing" : JSON.stringify(summary[0])} does not account for ${expected} selected tests; counting all as failed`)
+    }
+
+    for (const t of tests) {
+      if (t.suite === suite) resultsById.set(t.id, complete && !failed.has(t.id))
+    }
+  }
+  return resultsById
+}

+const suites = [...new Set(tests.map((t) => t.suite))]
